accepted.title: Review: Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game (PS5) - Solid Foundation Bending to Greatness
accepted.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game.
evidence_points: There have been plenty of video game adaptations of multimedia franchise Avatar: The Last Airbender , but Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game is the first to show any genuine promise.
Designed by Mike Zaimont of Skullgirls fame, this is a hand animated Street Fighter -esque one-on-one fighter with a more technical gameplay loop than you may be expecting.
Tutorials are weak so I had to spend a lot of time figuring out the basics, but effectively each of the title’s 12 included characters come with “Flow” abilities which determine how they play.
Some, like Katara, can zip around the stage on ice – closing distances and evading attacks at will. Others, like series protagonist Aang, can soar around the screen.
This all works in tandem with traditional fighting game combos, and it makes for a quite complex set of systems with a ton of potential.
You’ll be able to explore some of that in the character trials, where the game uses a DDR -style minigame to help you to get to grips with all of the different button inputs.
The game is quite innovative in this regard, but it feels half-baked – while it wants to show you the potential of each of the characters, it doesn’t really teach you the basics.

This can make getting through the single player campaign – a canon visual novel interspersed with combat sequences – a drag during difficulty spikes. I also had some trouble with the traditional arcade mode at times, too.

Online also lacks a ranked mode, meaning you’re pretty much at the mercy of matchmaking and are likely to get pummeled by some you play against. The netcode seems fine to me, but I’m not sure I really have the wherewithal to really master the mechanics here.
I do think the game looks and feels great, though: the animations are outstanding, and even the backgrounds are beautifully brought to life with lots of little details.

accepted.title: Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game Review | TheSixthAxis
accepted.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game.
evidence_points: I am someone who really enjoys the Avatar stories, the world that has been created, and of course the characters that inhabit it. Like many others, I have been waiting for a game to translate the setting of the show into a game that manages to capture what so many people have liked about the adventures of Aang and the trials of Korra. Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game, as you can probably guess, isn’t an action adventure or an RPG, but adapts the tale into a fighting game.

Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game captures the look and feel of the show well, from the animations to the characters and recognisable locations, including the likes of Ba Sing Se and the North Pole. The visuals in general are a strong point for the game, with the fights in motion looking generally smooth and action flowing well. The transitions between the different bending powers being used in battle, especially when the Avatar characters switch between them, are sublime. Watching the water, earth, air, and fire powers appear and be used in different ways by the different fighters is great. You can see the team has put in a lot of effort to making sure that the fighting movement flows well.

Like any fighting game, the animation and technical accuracy of hitboxes and netcode are fundamental, but the real satisfaction comes from digging into the roster and exploring their particular fighting styles. Avatar Legends launches with 12 playable fighters and some will be clear fan favourites while others will likely fall by the wayside. For me the faster movers like Korra, Katara, and Aang were my favourites, with the likes of Toph, Zuko, Zaheer, and Azula being close behind.

While Sokka is my favourite Avatar character, I didn’t really find him a particularly fun character to play as, along with Ozai and Kyoshi. Sokka’s lack of powers just limits how interesting his moveset can be, while Ozai and Kyoshi are slower moving characters that can be heavy hitters. Others will enjoy learning these characters and making them their mains, but they aren’t for me.

On the single player side of the Avatar Legends you have a training mode, arcade mode, and a story that is considered canon. To avoid clashes with The Last Airbender and The Legend of Korra, the game’s story takes place after the stories of both series have concluded, but in a realm where the worlds of Aang, Korra, and Kyoshi collide. The story is serviceable, but is not as strong as the series and while it has a bit of mystery to it, it isn’t something that hooks you.

The structure of story mode is also a bit weird. It consists of 27 chapters across three books, but some of the chapters are just one non-interactive scene and no fights, which pads the chapter count a fair bit. The story mode takes around four hours or so to complete, depending on your own skills – there’s some difficulty spikes as the opponent AI varies as well from unstoppable force to barely present. The former will trap you and juggle you at the edge of the screen while the latter will sometimes not move allowing you to get hits in. The majority of the fights though are decently balanced.
At the moment the multiplayer is still finding its feet and there is no ranked mode, so fights are unranked. There is local multiplayer as well too.

accepted.title: Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game — IGN review
accepted.identity_evidence: Critic review for Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game attributed by Metacritic to IGN.
evidence_points: The potential of Avatar Legends is immense. This is a gorgeous 2D fighting game that excels as both a throwback to the bygone era of sprite-based fighters and a faithful adaptation of the beloved cartoons it’s based on. It’s got some of the most satisfying movement of any 2D fighter I’ve played, combos routes that are challenging but immensely rewarding to learn, a 12 character roster that feels way bigger than it actually is thanks to the clever support system, and flexible combat that allows for a ton of creative expression. The lackluster story mode and complete absence of some basic options like difficulty settings for the CPU certainly make Avatar Legends hard to recommend to casual Ava

accepted.title: Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game — Shacknews review
accepted.identity_evidence: Critic review for Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game attributed by Metacritic to Shacknews.
evidence_points: Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game is a rock-solid fighter that manages to honor a beloved IP without compromising any of the sensibilities needed to succeed in this genre. The characters are interesting (even if the game could use more), and the skill ceiling feels incredibly high. Like the Avatar, a long journey lies ahead for players eager to master the elements.
